outcomes: No more guessing whether the work is good enough
Accessibility no longer Todd's solo burden
Compliant with Colorado's accessibility law and federal Title II requirements
Critical barriers fixed first, everything else follows
aria_label_2: Visit the Kit Carson County official website
heading_7: “I feel like I'm trying to keep the Titanic afloat with a spoon.”
paragraph_8: That's Todd Holmes, IT support specialist at Kit Carson County. His title on paper: one. His actual job: five public systems.
paragraph_9: When Colorado made website accessibility the law, it landed on his desk too.
heading_10: He was already doing real accessibility work.
paragraph_11: Todd tagged every site image by hand. He added automated PDF tagging. He held back documents that failed quality checks. He was doing genuinely good work.
paragraph_12: But he had no idea if it was enough.
paragraph_13: “Are we there? No. I'm doing the best I can. Is it going to be good enough? I don't know.”
text_14: Todd Holmes, IT Support Specialist, Kit Carson County
paragraph_15: Not neglect. A capable person doing real work with no clarity on whether he was meeting Colorado's requirements.
paragraph_17: Auditing a site and fixing what it finds is expensive. And it is never a one-time job.
paragraph_18: Websites change. New content gets added. Pages get updated. Every change has the potential to introduce a new barrier, so the work has to keep going.
paragraph_20: “The cost of it was just ridiculous. So not doing that. At that point, it's cheaper to pay the fine.”
paragraph_23: A3S is a monthly program that handles continuous auditing, remediating, and validating. Every month. Built into the operating budget.
paragraph_24: Todd got continuous compliance without breaking the bank.
heading_25: Todd still runs IT for the whole county. Accessibility just isn't his alone anymore.
paragraph_26: A3S runs the county's accessibility audit cycle every month. Each cycle produces the same evidence: tested pages, barriers found, fixes applied, verification complete.
paragraph_27: That documented record is the proof Colorado requires. Todd's answer changed from “I don't know” to “I have proof.”
alt_29: Sunset over an open prairie of wild sunflowers
paragraph_31: “Don't know where I would be without you.”
paragraph_34: Colorado and Title II both require continuous compliance and documented proof. Most counties are doing the work but struggling to prove it meets either standard. Kit Carson County now has evidence every month.
paragraph_36: Both Colorado penalties and Title II violations carry real costs. Most counties are caught between doing the work and proving they're compliant. Kit Carson County demonstrates compliance to both.
paragraph_37: We'll spend an hour looking at your site, at no cost.
paragraph_38: You will see exactly where you stand.
